title: DSA core: two pointers, window, stack and binary search
seriesDescription: Complexity and pattern reasoning for hashing, windows, stacks, lists, trees, heaps and graphs, in pseudocode. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Language-independent reasoning for sliding window, monotonic stack and binary search: pattern recognition, amortised cost, search on the answer, and worked integer problems.
source: LeetCode problem set; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview; CLRS (binary search, amortised analysis)

questions.prompt: Match each problem with the technique that solves it best.

right.text: Sliding window with a last-seen map
Sort, then fix one element and run two pointers

questions.explanation: Pattern recognition is the interview skill: window for contiguous ranges with a constraint, two pointers on sorted input, stack for nesting, monotonic stack for next greater, binary search on a monotonic yes/no answer.

questions.prompt: This longest-substring-without-repeats loop sets left = last[c] + 1 whenever c was seen before (it forgets max(left, ...)). What does it return for "abba", whose correct answer is 2?
questions.explanation: Walk it: a, b give length 2; the second b moves left to 2; the final a was last seen at 0, so left jumps back to 1 and the window "bba" looks like length 3. The max(left, ...) keeps left from moving backwards.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A sliding window loop with an inner while that moves the left pointer is still O(n) overall.
questions.reason: Each of the two pointers only moves forward and travels at most n positions in total.

whys.a: Correct: total pointer moves are at most 2n, so the nested loop is amortised linear.
whys.b: R is the actual reason, so "does not explain" is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c cannot be right.
whys.d: A is true, so d cannot be right.

questions.explanation: Amortised analysis counts total work across the whole run, not per iteration of the outer loop.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A monotonic stack finds the next greater element for every item of an array in O(n) total time.
questions.reason: A stack push and a stack pop each take O(1) time.

whys.a: R only covers the cost of one stack operation, not the total number of operations.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but the linear bound comes from every index being pushed once and popped at most once; constant-time operations alone do not give it.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Each element enters the stack once and leaves once, so the inner while loop does at most n pops across the whole scan.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Binary search on the answer for Koko runs in O(n log M), where M is the largest pile.
questions.reason: The piles array must be sorted before the search can run.

whys.a: A is true but R is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.b: R is false: the piles can stay in any order; only the feasibility check is monotonic.
whys.c: Correct: the O(n log M) bound holds, but the search is over speeds 1..M and needs a monotonic feasible(k) predicate, not a sorted piles array.
whys.d: A is true (log M iterations, each an O(n) feasibility scan), so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Binary search works on any monotonic yes/no predicate, not only on sorted arrays.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Binary search finds a value that is present in any array.
questions.reason: Binary search compares the middle element with the target at every step.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: R is true, but the halving logic only works when the array is sorted, so A is false for an unsorted array.

questions.explanation: If the input is unsorted and you search once, a linear scan is O(n) and cheaper than sorting first.

questions.prompt: Complete the description of next greater element.
questions.text: Scan left to right keeping a monotonic {1} stack of {2}; while the new value is bigger than the one on top, {3} the stack and record the answer for it.
questions.explanation: Storing indices (not values) lets you write the answer into the right output slot and compute distances.

questions.prompt: What is the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram with bar heights [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]?
questions.explanation: Bars 5 and 6 side by side give height 5 and width 2, so 10. The alternatives are smaller: height 2 across four bars is 8, height 1 across six bars is 6. A monotonic increasing stack finds it in O(n).

questions.prompt: What is the total water trapped by the elevation map [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1]?
questions.explanation: Each cell holds min(max to its left, max to its right) minus its own height; summing gives 6. Two pointers computes it in O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.prompt: What is the length of the shortest substring of s = "ADOBECODEBANC" that contains every letter of t = "ABC" (with multiplicity)?
questions.explanation: The window "BANC" has length 4. Expand the right edge until all of t is covered, then shrink the left edge while it stays covered.

questions.prompt: In the worst case, how many midpoints are examined to find or rule out a value in a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements, with standard binary search making one probe per iteration?
questions.explanation: Each probe halves the range, and 2^19 = 524,288 < 1,000,000 <= 2^20 - 1 = 1,048,575 gives at most 20 probes: floor(log2 n) + 1.

questions.prompt: Koko must eat all piles within h hours at speed k bananas per hour (each hour she eats from one pile). Why can you binary search k?

options.text: Feasibility is monotonic in k: a faster speed never hurts.
options.why: Correct: if speed k finishes in time, any larger speed also does, so feasible(k) flips from false to true once.

options.text: The piles array can be sorted first, which enables the search.
options.why: Sorting is not needed and does not create the monotonic property.

options.text: The total number of bananas is always an exact power of two.
options.why: Nothing in the problem makes the total a power of two.

options.text: The hours needed is a convex function of the eating speed.
options.why: Convexity is not the requirement; a monotonic yes/no predicate is.

questions.explanation: Recognise "find the minimum value for which a monotonic predicate holds" as binary search on the answer: capacity of a ship, split array, minimum speed.

questions.prompt: When searching a rotated sorted array without duplicates, such as [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], how do you decide which half is sorted at each step?

options.text: Compare a[mid] with the target only, ignoring a[lo] and a[hi].
options.why: Without the endpoints you cannot tell which side the target lies on.

options.text: Find the maximum first with a linear scan, then split there.
options.why: A scan makes the whole search O(n), defeating the point.

options.text: Always search the left half first, then fall back to the right.
options.why: That degrades to a full traversal instead of halving the range.

options.text: If a[lo] <= a[mid] the left half is sorted, else the right.
options.why: Correct: one half of any split is always in order, and this comparison tells you which.

questions.explanation: After you know which half is sorted, check whether the target lies inside that half's range and keep that half, otherwise keep the other.

questions.prompt: To support push, pop, top and getMin all in O(1), what should a min-stack store?

options.text: One variable holding the smallest value pushed so far, updated on each push.
options.why: After the minimum is popped this variable cannot be restored.

options.text: Alongside each pushed value, the minimum of the stack at that moment.
options.why: Correct: popping then restores the previous minimum automatically.

options.text: A sorted list of every value, updated on each push and on each pop.
options.why: Keeping a list sorted costs O(n) per update, not O(1).

options.text: A min-heap kept alongside the stack and polled whenever getMin is called.
options.why: Polling a heap removes the minimum and costs O(log n).

questions.explanation: Each stack entry carries its own running minimum, so every operation is O(1).

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode that returns the first index i with a[i] >= x in a sorted array a (the length of a if there is none), using a half-open range [lo, hi).

checks.label: starts with lo = 0 and hi = length
moves lo to mid + 1 when a[mid] < x
sets hi = mid otherwise and returns lo

questions.explanation: Everything left of lo is < x and everything from hi on is >= x, so when the range closes lo is the answer. The same template finds the first true of any monotonic predicate.
